questions.sec: General Features of Asthma, the Bronchodilator Reversibility Box, GINA Features and Respiratory Symptoms with Triggers
questions.q: Which five features of Asthma head the chapter on page 243?
opts: Pure airway disease; no parenchymal involvement, so no hypercapnia, pulmonary HTN or cor-pulmonale; chronic; inflammatory (eosinophils); and irreversible bronchoconstriction
Pure airway disease; no parenchymal involvement, so no hypercapnia, pulmonary HTN or cor-pulmonale; chronic; inflammatory (eosinophils); and reversible bronchoconstriction
Pure airway disease; parenchymal involvement, so hypercapnia and cor-pulmonale; chronic; inflammatory (eosinophils); and reversible bronchoconstriction
Pure parenchymal disease; no parenchymal involvement, so no hypercapnia, pulmonary HTN or cor-pulmonale; acute; inflammatory (neutrophils); and reversible bronchoconstriction
questions.exp: The bullets read 'Pure airway disease', 'No parenchymal involvement → No hypercapnia, pulmonary HTN, cor-pulmonale', 'Chronic', 'Inflammatory (Eosinophils)' and 'Reversible bronchoconstriction', echoing the asthma exception in the Type I table on page 230. (Book p243)

questions.sec: General Features of Asthma, the Bronchodilator Reversibility Box, GINA Features and Respiratory Symptoms with Triggers
questions.q: Which numbers does the bronchodilator reversibility box print on page 243?
opts: Four puffs of SABA, reassessed at 30 minutes, with FEV1 rising by 12% plus a 200 ml rise in absolute value
Four puffs of LABA, reassessed at 30 minutes, with FEV1 rising by 12% plus a 200 ml rise in absolute value
Four puffs of SABA, reassessed at 30 minutes, with FEV1 rising by 15% plus a 250 ml rise in absolute value
Two puffs of SABA, reassessed at 15 minutes, with FEV1 rising by 12% plus a 200 ml rise in absolute value
questions.exp: The box reads 'On bronchodilator reversibility testing: (4 puffs of SABA) — 30 mins — FEV1: ↑ by 12% + 200 ml ↑ in absolute value.' Both the percentage and the absolute rise must be met. (Book p243)

questions.sec: General Features of Asthma, the Bronchodilator Reversibility Box, GINA Features and Respiratory Symptoms with Triggers
questions.q: Match each reversibility result in the page 243 box with its printed label — 1) Rise present, marked plus 2) Rise absent, marked minus … A) Irreversible, labelled COPD B) Reversible, labelled Asthma
questions.exp: The box splits into '+' leading to 'Reversible (Asthma)' and '−' leading to 'Irreversible (COPD)'. The same 12% and 200 ml rule separated asthma from COPD on page 199. (Book p243)

questions.sec: General Features of Asthma, the Bronchodilator Reversibility Box, GINA Features and Respiratory Symptoms with Triggers
questions.q: Which three components are stacked as the GINA features of Asthma on page 243?
opts: Chronic airway inflammation with reversible bronchoconstriction, plus variable expiratory air-flow obstruction, plus parenchymal destruction
Chronic airway inflammation with irreversible bronchoconstriction, plus fixed expiratory air-flow obstruction, plus symptoms due to broncho-constriction
Acute airway inflammation with reversible bronchoconstriction, plus variable inspiratory air-flow obstruction, plus symptoms due to broncho-constriction
Chronic airway inflammation with reversible bronchoconstriction, plus variable expiratory air-flow obstruction, plus symptoms due to broncho-constriction
questions.exp: Under 'GINA (Global initiative for Asthma) features of asthma' the page stacks chronic airway inflammation with reversible bronchoconstriction, variable expiratory air-flow obstruction and symptoms due to broncho-constriction, joined by plus signs. (Book p243)

questions.sec: General Features of Asthma, the Bronchodilator Reversibility Box, GINA Features and Respiratory Symptoms with Triggers
questions.q: The four symptoms printed as due to broncho-constriction are shortness of breath, chronic cough, wheeze and ______.
opts: hemoptysis
chest pain
stridor
chest tightness
questions.exp: The bracket reads '(Shortness of breath/chronic cough/wheeze/chest tightness)'. Chest tightness, not pleuritic chest pain, is the fourth GINA symptom printed here. (Book p243)

questions.sec: General Features of Asthma, the Bronchodilator Reversibility Box, GINA Features and Respiratory Symptoms with Triggers
questions.q: How do the respiratory symptoms of Asthma behave, according to the foot of page 243?
opts: They are variable in time and intensity, worse at night and with viral infections (influenza most common as printed)
They are variable in time and intensity, worse at night and with bacterial infections (pneumococcus most common)
They are variable in time and intensity, worse at night and with viral infections (RSV most common)
They are fixed in time and intensity, worse in the morning and with viral infections (RSV most common)
questions.exp: The bullets read 'variable in time and intensity' and 'worse: At night. With viral infections (RSV: m/c).' RSV is the organism named in brackets. (Book p243)

questions.sec: General Features of Asthma, the Bronchodilator Reversibility Box, GINA Features and Respiratory Symptoms with Triggers
questions.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — three of these are printed triggers of Asthma symptoms on page 243, one appears only in the next day's trigger list on page 244:
opts: Paint fumes
Exercise
Cold air
Laughter
questions.exp: Page 243 closes with 'Triggers: Exercise, laughter, allergens, cold air.' Paint fumes belongs to the separate etiopathogenesis trigger list on page 244, alongside sulfur dioxide and beta blockers. (Book p243)

questions.sec: General Features of Asthma, the Bronchodilator Reversibility Box, GINA Features and Respiratory Symptoms with Triggers
questions.q: A patient's FEV1 rises 14% and 240 ml thirty minutes after four puffs of SABA. Using the page 243 box alone, how is this labelled?
opts: Indeterminate, because only the percentage criterion is printed
Reversible — labelled Asthma
Irreversible — labelled COPD
Reversible — labelled COPD
questions.exp: Both printed thresholds are exceeded (12% and 200 ml in absolute value at 30 minutes after 4 puffs of SABA), so the '+' arm applies: 'Reversible (Asthma)'. A sub-threshold rise would take the '−' arm to COPD. (Book p243)

questions.sec: Etiopathogenesis: Triggers, Hygiene Hypothesis and TH2 Cytokines, Early versus Late Phases, and Eosinophil Mediators and Granules
questions.q: What etiology and trigger list open the etiopathogenesis on page 244?
opts: Etiology unknown; triggers upper respiratory infection (URI), aspirin, beta blockers, sulfur dioxide, paint fumes, obesity, diet, 5q polymorphism and hyperventilation
Etiology unknown; triggers lower respiratory infection, aspirin, beta blockers, carbon dioxide, paint fumes, obesity, diet, 5q polymorphism and hyperventilation
Etiology allergic; triggers upper respiratory infection (URI), aspirin, beta agonists, sulfur dioxide, paint fumes, obesity, diet, 5q polymorphism and hyperventilation
Etiology unknown; triggers upper respiratory infection (URI), aspirin, beta blockers, sulfur dioxide, paint fumes, obesity, diet, 17q polymorphism and hypoventilation
questions.exp: The section reads 'Etiology: unknown' and lists triggers in two columns: URI, aspirin, beta blockers, sulfur dioxide, paint fumes, and obesity, diet, 5q polymorphism, hyperventilation. Beta blockers, not agonists, are the drug trigger. (Book p244)

questions.sec: Etiopathogenesis: Triggers, Hygiene Hypothesis and TH2 Cytokines, Early versus Late Phases, and Eosinophil Mediators and Granules
questions.q: Which chain states the hygiene hypothesis on page 244?
opts: Increased exposure to antigens in adulthood promotes conversion of TH2 to TH1 cells, giving better immunity
Increased exposure to antigens in childhood promotes conversion of TH2 to TH1 cells, giving better immunity
Increased exposure to antigens in childhood promotes conversion of TH1 to TH2 cells, giving better immunity
Decreased exposure to antigens in childhood promotes conversion of TH2 to TH1 cells, giving better immunity
questions.exp: The bullet reads '↑ exposure to antigens in childhood → Promotes conversion of TH2 to TH1 cells → Better immunity.' The conversion runs away from the TH2 phenotype that drives Asthma. (Book p244)

questions.sec: Etiopathogenesis: Triggers, Hygiene Hypothesis and TH2 Cytokines, Early versus Late Phases, and Eosinophil Mediators and Granules
questions.q: Match each TH2 product on page 244 with its printed action — 1) IL-4 2) IL-5 3) IL-13 … A) Listed with no action printed against it B) Recruits eosinophils via eotaxin C) Raises IgE
questions.exp: Under 'TH2 produces' the page gives 'IL-4: ↑ IgE', 'IL-5: Recruits eosinophils via eotaxin' and 'IL-13' with no action printed. These are the same three cytokines named for eosinophilic inflammation in ABPA on page 254. (Book p244)

questions.sec: Etiopathogenesis: Triggers, Hygiene Hypothesis and TH2 Cytokines, Early versus Late Phases, and Eosinophil Mediators and Granules
questions.q: Match each Asthma phase with its printed timing and mediators — 1) Early phase response 2) Late phase … A) After 4–6 hours, mediator listed as basophil B) Mediators histamine, tryptase and PGD2
questions.exp: The Phases block pairs the early phase response with mediators histamine, tryptase and PGD2, and the 'Late phase (After 4–6 hrs)' with basophil as its listed mediator entry. (Book p244)

questions.sec: Etiopathogenesis: Triggers, Hygiene Hypothesis and TH2 Cytokines, Early versus Late Phases, and Eosinophil Mediators and Granules
questions.q: TRUE or FALSE about the phases printed on page 244.
opts: True — the late phase is timed after 4–6 hours and its mediator entry is the basophil, while histamine, tryptase and PGD2 belong to the early phase
False — histamine and tryptase are printed as late-phase mediators
True — the early phase mediator entry is the basophil and PGD2 is a late mediator
False — the late phase is timed after 24 hours on this page
questions.exp: The block is explicit: 'Late phase (After 4–6 hrs)' arrows down to 'Basophil', and the early phase column lists histamine, tryptase and PGD2. Swapping either column contradicts the print. (Book p244)

questions.sec: Etiopathogenesis: Triggers, Hygiene Hypothesis and TH2 Cytokines, Early versus Late Phases, and Eosinophil Mediators and Granules
questions.q: Which mediators form the eosinophil's newly synthesised membrane-derived set on page 244?
opts: Leukotriene B4, platelet activating factor, 15 HETE, prostaglandin D2, and thromboxane A2
Leukotriene B4, platelet activating factor, 15 HETE, prostaglandin E1 and E2, and thromboxane B2
Leukotriene C4, platelet activating factor, 15 HETE, prostaglandin E1 and E2, and thromboxane B2
Leukotriene B4, histamine, 15 HETE, prostaglandin E1 and E2, and thromboxane B2
questions.exp: The upper arrow from the eosinophil diagram reads 'Newly synthesised membrane derived mediators: Leukotriene B4, Platelet activating factor, 15 HETE, Prostaglandin E1, E2, Thromboxane B2.' PGD2 was an early-phase mediator in the block above. (Book p244)

questions.sec: Etiopathogenesis: Triggers, Hygiene Hypothesis and TH2 Cytokines, Early versus Late Phases, and Eosinophil Mediators and Granules
questions.q: Which four granule-derived basic proteins are listed from the eosinophil diagram?
opts: Major basic protein (MBP), eosinophil anionic protein (ECP), eosinophil derived neurotoxin (EDN) and eosinophil peroxidase (EPO)
Minor basic protein (MBP), eosinophil cationic protein (ECP), eosinophil derived neurotoxin (EDN) and eosinophil peroxidase (EPO)
Major basic protein (MBP), eosinophil cationic protein (ECP), eosinophil derived neurotoxin (EDN) and Charcot Leyden protein
Major basic protein (MBP), eosinophil cationic protein (ECP), eosinophil derived neurotoxin (EDN) and eosinophil peroxidase (EPO)
questions.exp: The lower arrow reads 'Granule derived basic proteins: major basic protein (MBP), Eosinophil cationic protein (ECP), Eosinophil derived neurotoxin (EDN), Eosinophil peroxidase (EPO).' Charcot Leyden material is handled separately as a granule type. (Book p244)

questions.sec: Etiopathogenesis: Triggers, Hygiene Hypothesis and TH2 Cytokines, Early versus Late Phases, and Eosinophil Mediators and Granules
questions.q: Of the two granule types in eosinophils, the 1° (primary) granules give ______, while the 2° granules contain MBP, ECP and EDN.
opts: Masson's buds
Birbeck granules
Charcot Leyden crystals
Curschmann spirals
questions.exp: The side box reads '1° granules: Charcot Leyden crystals. 2° granules: MBP, ECP, EDN.' Curschmann spirals are a histopathology finding on the next page, not a granule product here. (Book p244)

questions.sec: Histopathology of Asthma with Curschmann Spirals, the Extrinsic versus Intrinsic Table and Samter's Triad
questions.q: Which four numbered headings make up the histopathology of Asthma on page 245?
opts: Acute airway inflammation; bronchial smooth muscle hypertrophy; submucosal glandular (goblet cell) hypoplasia; and patchy necrosis of epithelium
Chronic airway inflammation; bronchial smooth muscle atrophy; submucosal glandular (goblet cell) hyperplasia; and diffuse necrosis of epithelium
Chronic airway inflammation; bronchial smooth muscle hypertrophy; submucosal glandular (goblet cell) hyperplasia; and patchy necrosis of epithelium
Chronic airway inflammation; bronchial cartilage hypertrophy; submucosal glandular (goblet cell) hyperplasia; and patchy necrosis of endothelium
questions.exp: The numbered list reads '1. Chronic airway inflammation, 2. Bronchial smooth muscle hypertrophy, 3. Submucosal glandular (Goblet cell) hyperplasia, 4. Patchy necrosis of epithelium.' Muscle hypertrophies and glands hyperplase; the necrosis is patchy and epithelial. (Book p245)

questions.sec: Histopathology of Asthma with Curschmann Spirals, the Extrinsic versus Intrinsic Table and Samter's Triad
questions.q: Which five elements are listed inside chronic airway inflammation, and which one captions the micrograph?
opts: Eosinophils, mucus plugs, mast cells, Curschmann spirals and Charcot Leyden crystals — with the image captioned Charcot Leyden crystals
Eosinophils, mucus plugs, mast cells, Curschmann spirals and Charcot Leyden crystals — with the image captioned Curschmann spirals
Neutrophils, mucus plugs, mast cells, Curschmann spirals and Charcot Leyden crystals — with the image captioned Curschmann spirals
Eosinophils, mucus plugs, basophils, Masson's buds and Charcot Leyden crystals — with the image captioned Curschmann spirals
questions.exp: Under chronic airway inflammation the bullets are eosinophils, mucus plugs, mast cells, Curschmann spirals and Charcot Leyden crystals, and the red micrograph beside them is captioned 'Curschmann spirals'. (Book p245)

questions.sec: Histopathology of Asthma with Curschmann Spirals, the Extrinsic versus Intrinsic Table and Samter's Triad
questions.q: Match each row of the extrinsic versus intrinsic table with its printed pair — 1) Association with allergy and skin tests 2) Serum IgE 3) Family history 4) Prognosis … A) Extrinsic raised, intrinsic normal B) Extrinsic good with children growing out of Asthma, intrinsic poor C) Extrinsic positive, intrinsic negative D) Extrinsic present, intrinsic absent
questions.exp: The table gives extrinsic/atopic Asthma '+' for allergy association and skin tests against '−' for intrinsic, S. IgE '↑' versus 'Normal', family history '+' versus 'Absent', and prognosis 'Good (Children grow out of asthma)' versus 'Poor'. (Book p245)

questions.sec: Histopathology of Asthma with Curschmann Spirals, the Extrinsic versus Intrinsic Table and Samter's Triad
questions.q: Match each remaining table row with its printed extrinsic versus intrinsic pair — 1) Etiology 2) Age of onset 3) Gender predisposition 4) Degree and triggers … A) Childhood onset with peak age 3 years versus adult onset B) Dermatophagoids, the house dust mite, as most common organism versus staphylococcal enterotoxins C) Dashes for extrinsic versus severe persistent degree and respiratory infection triggers for intrinsic D) M equal to F versus M greater than F
questions.exp: Etiology pairs 'm/c organism: Dermatophagoids (House dust mite)' with 'Staphylococcal enterotoxins'; onset pairs childhood (peak 3 yrs) with adult; gender pairs 'm = F' with 'm > F'; and the degree and trigger rows carry dashes for extrinsic against 'Severe, persistent' and 'Respiratory infections' for intrinsic. (Book p245)

questions.sec: Histopathology of Asthma with Curschmann Spirals, the Extrinsic versus Intrinsic Table and Samter's Triad
questions.q: Which single age figure is printed anywhere in the extrinsic versus intrinsic table?
opts: Peak age 13 years, attached to childhood-onset extrinsic/atopic Asthma
Peak age 30 years, attached to childhood-onset extrinsic/atopic Asthma
Peak age 3 years, attached to childhood-onset extrinsic/atopic Asthma
Peak age 3 years, attached to adult-onset intrinsic Asthma
questions.exp: The age-of-onset cell reads 'Childhood onset (Peak age: 3 yrs)' for extrinsic/atopic Asthma against 'Adult onset' for intrinsic Asthma. Three years is the table's only age. (Book p245)

questions.sec: Histopathology of Asthma with Curschmann Spirals, the Extrinsic versus Intrinsic Table and Samter's Triad
questions.q: An adult man with no family history, normal serum IgE, negative skin tests and severe persistent Asthma triggered by respiratory infections is discussed. Which column of the page 245 table does he fill, and what prognosis does it carry?
opts: Intrinsic Asthma — prognosis poor
Extrinsic/atopic Asthma — prognosis good, as children grow out of Asthma
Intrinsic Asthma — prognosis good, as children grow out of Asthma
Extrinsic/atopic Asthma — prognosis poor
questions.exp: Adult onset, absent family history, normal IgE, negative skin tests, male predominance, severe persistent degree and respiratory-infection triggers are the intrinsic column cell by cell, whose prognosis row reads 'Poor'. (Book p245)

questions.sec: Histopathology of Asthma with Curschmann Spirals, the Extrinsic versus Intrinsic Table and Samter's Triad
questions.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — three of these form the captioned triangle at the foot of page 245, one does not:
opts: Nasal polyps
Childhood onset Asthma
Adult onset Asthma
Aspirin sensitivity
questions.exp: The Note 'Samters triad' (as printed) draws a triangle of adult onset Asthma at the apex with aspirin sensitivity and nasal polyps at the base corners. Childhood onset belongs to extrinsic Asthma in the table above. (Book p245)

questions.sec: Histopathology of Asthma with Curschmann Spirals, the Extrinsic versus Intrinsic Table and Samter's Triad
questions.q: The triangle of adult onset Asthma, aspirin sensitivity and nasal polyps is labelled ______ triad (spelling as printed).
opts: Kartagener's
Widal's printed as Vidal's
Virchow's
Samters
questions.exp: The Note is headed 'Samters triad', without an apostrophe, exactly as printed on page 245. Aspirin also appears as a trigger on page 244, tying the triad back to the etiopathogenesis list. (Book p245)

questions.sec: Mild versus Moderate versus Severe Asthma Table and Acute Severe Exacerbation versus Impending Respiratory Failure
questions.q: Which symptom-pattern scheme introduces the severity grading on page 246?
opts: Asthma with intermittent symptoms grades into mild and moderate only, while severe Asthma is separately defined
Asthma with persistent symptoms stands apart, while Asthma with intermittent symptoms grades into mild, moderate and severe
Asthma with nocturnal symptoms grades into mild, moderate and severe
Asthma with intermittent symptoms stands apart, while Asthma with persistent symptoms grades into mild, moderate and severe
questions.exp: Under 'B. mild v/s moderate v/s severe' the arrows read 'Asthma with → Intermittent symptoms' and '→ Persistent symptoms → mild, moderate, Severe'. The three grades subdivide persistent disease only. (Book p246)

questions.sec: Mild versus Moderate versus Severe Asthma Table and Acute Severe Exacerbation versus Impending Respiratory Failure
questions.q: Reading the severity table by column position (mild, then moderate, then severe), which day-symptom and FEV1 ladder is printed?
opts: Day symptoms 2–6 days/week, then continuous, then daily; FEV1 above 80% predicted, then below 60% predicted, then 60–80% predicted
Day symptoms 2–6 days/week, then daily, then continuous; FEV1 above 80% predicted, then 60–80% predicted, then below 60% predicted
Day symptoms daily, then 2–6 days/week, then continuous; FEV1 above 80% predicted, then 60–80% predicted, then below 60% predicted
Day symptoms 2–6 days/week, then daily, then continuous; FEV1 below 60% predicted, then 60–80% predicted, then above 80% predicted
questions.exp: The columns run '2–6 days/week, Daily, Continuous' for day symptoms and '>80% predicted, 60–80% predicted, <60% predicted' for FEV1. Note the print carries over the headers 'Extrinsic/atopic' and 'Intrinsic' from page 245 over the moderate and severe columns, so the grades are read by position under the 'mild v/s moderate v/s severe' heading. (Book p246)

questions.sec: Mild versus Moderate versus Severe Asthma Table and Acute Severe Exacerbation versus Impending Respiratory Failure
questions.q: Which nocturnal-awakening and PEFR-variability cells complete that table?
opts: Nocturnal awakenings more than 2 monthly, then more than 1 per week, then 'Significantly ↓ activity' as printed in the third cell; PEFR variability below 30%, then above 30%, then above 30%
Nocturnal awakenings more than 2 monthly, then more than 1 per week, then 'Significantly ↓ activity' as printed in the third cell; PEFR variability above 30%, then below 30%, then below 30%
Nocturnal awakenings more than 2 monthly, then more than 1 per week, then frequent; PEFR variability below 30%, then above 30%, then below 30%
Nocturnal awakenings more than 2 weekly, then more than 1 monthly, then nightly; PEFR variability below 30%, then above 30%, then above 30%
questions.exp: The rows read '>2 monthly, >1/week, Significantly ↓ activity' for nocturnal awakenings — the third cell describing activity rather than awakenings, preserved as printed — and '<30%, >30%, >30%' for PEFR variability. (Book p246)

questions.sec: Mild versus Moderate versus Severe Asthma Table and Acute Severe Exacerbation versus Impending Respiratory Failure
questions.q: Match each bedside row with its acute-exacerbation versus impending-failure pair on page 246 — 1) Speech 2) Orientation 3) Position 4) Accessory muscle use and loud wheeze … A) Upright versus cannot recline B) Both marked ++ in exacerbation versus paradoxical breathing and a silent chest in impending failure C) Words versus absent D) Agitated versus confused
questions.exp: In acute exacerbation speech is in 'Words', orientation 'Agitated', position 'upright', and accessory muscle use and loud wheeze are '++'; in impending respiratory failure speech is 'Absent', orientation 'Confused', position 'Cant recline', accessory use becomes 'Paradoxical breathing' and wheeze is '− (Silent chest)'. Breathlessness at rest and tachypnoea carry a merged '+' across both columns. (Book p246)

questions.sec: Mild versus Moderate versus Severe Asthma Table and Acute Severe Exacerbation versus Impending Respiratory Failure
questions.q: Match each physiological row with its printed pair in the same table — 1) Heart rate 2) Pulsus paradoxus 3) PEFR 4) PaO2 and PaCO2 … A) 25–40 L/min as printed versus below 25 L/min B) Marked ++ versus absent C) Merged cells across both columns: PaO2 below 60 mmHg (saturation below 90%) and PaCO2 below 40 mmHg D) Tachycardia versus relative bradycardia
questions.exp: Heart rate moves from tachycardia to relative bradycardia and pulsus paradoxus from '++' to absent as failure impends; PEFR falls from '25–40 L/min' to '<25 L/min' (units as printed), while PaO2 '<60 mmHg (<90%)' and PaCO2 '<40 mmHg' are merged across both columns. (Book p246)

questions.sec: Mild versus Moderate versus Severe Asthma Table and Acute Severe Exacerbation versus Impending Respiratory Failure
questions.q: A breathless asthmatic can no longer speak, is confused, cannot recline, has paradoxical breathing, a silent chest, relative bradycardia and no pulsus paradoxus, with PEFR under the lower printed band. Which column has he crossed into?
opts: Mild persistent Asthma
Intermittent Asthma
Acute exacerbation of Asthma
Impending respiratory failure
questions.exp: Absent speech, confusion, inability to recline, paradoxical breathing, silent chest, relative bradycardia, absent pulsus paradoxus and PEFR below 25 (printed L/min) are the impending respiratory failure column cell by cell. (Book p246)

questions.sec: Mild versus Moderate versus Severe Asthma Table and Acute Severe Exacerbation versus Impending Respiratory Failure
questions.q: TRUE or FALSE about the merged cells of the exacerbation table on page 246.
opts: False — breathlessness at rest is printed only under impending respiratory failure
True — breathlessness at rest and tachypnoea each carry a single '+' merged across both columns, as do the PaO2 and PaCO2 values
False — PaCO2 is given as above 40 mmHg in impending failure
True — loud wheeze is also merged across both columns with a single '++'
questions.exp: The breathlessness-at-rest and tachypnoea rows show one '+' spanning exacerbation and impending failure, and the gas rows merge as PaO2 '<60 mmHg (<90%)' with PaCO2 '<40 mmHg'. Loud wheeze, by contrast, splits '++' against the silent chest. (Book p246)

questions.sec: Management: Inhaled Corticosteroids as Mainstay, the ICS–Formoterol Step Protocol with Biologics, and Investigations
questions.q: Which status, effects and examples are printed for inhaled corticosteroids on page 247?
opts: Mainstay of treatment; effects of reduced hospitalisations, exacerbations and symptoms with improved lung functions, early administration improving future lung function; examples beclomethasone, budesonide and fluticasone
Mainstay of treatment; effects of reduced hospitalisations and symptoms only; examples beclomethasone, budesonide and prednisolone

Mainstay of treatment; effects of reduced hospitalisations, exacerbations and symptoms with improved lung functions, early administration improving future lung function; examples salmeterol, budesonide and fluticasone
Reliever of choice; effects of reduced hospitalisations, exacerbations and symptoms with improved lung functions; examples beclomethasone, budesonide and fluticasone
questions.exp: The ICS block reads 'mainstay of treatment' with effects '↓ Hospitalisations, ↓ exacerbations, ↓ symptoms, Improved lung functions, early ICS administration → Improved lung function in future' and examples beclomethasone, budesonide and fluticasone. 'ICS' is misprinted once as 'LCS' in the early-administration line, preserved in the caveat record. (Book p247)

questions.sec: Management: Inhaled Corticosteroids as Mainstay, the ICS–Formoterol Step Protocol with Biologics, and Investigations
questions.q: Complete the printed Note: Short acting β agonists (SABA) has ______ in persistent Asthma.
opts: an equal role with ICS
no role
a reliever-only role
the mainstay role
questions.exp: The Note reads 'Short acting β agonists (SABA) has no role in persistent asthma', which is why the protocol below is built entirely on ICS–formoterol combinations. (Book p247)

questions.sec: Management: Inhaled Corticosteroids as Mainstay, the ICS–Formoterol Step Protocol with Biologics, and Investigations
questions.q: Which opening steps does the page 247 protocol print before any dose escalation?
opts: As-and-when-needed SABA first, then daily low-dose ICS plus formoterol, printed as better than daily low-dose ICS alone
Daily low-dose ICS alone first, then as-and-when-needed ICS–formoterol combination
As-and-when-needed ICS–formoterol combination first, then daily low-dose ICS plus salmeterol
As-and-when-needed ICS–formoterol combination first, then daily low-dose ICS plus formoterol, printed as better than daily low-dose ICS alone
questions.exp: The flowchart opens 'As and when needed ICS-Formoterol combo' and descends to 'Daily low-dose ICS + Formoterol > Daily low dose ICS', the inequality making the combination the preferred daily step. (Book p247)

questions.sec: Management: Inhaled Corticosteroids as Mainstay, the ICS–Formoterol Step Protocol with Biologics, and Investigations
questions.q: A patient remains uncontrolled on daily low-dose ICS–formoterol. Which printed sequence follows?
opts: High-dose ICS plus formoterol at once; then add tiotropium, the short-acting muscarinic antagonist
Medium-dose ICS alone; if still not responding, oral steroids; then add tiotropium
Medium-dose ICS plus formoterol; if still not responding, high-dose ICS plus formoterol; then add tiotropium, the long-acting muscarinic antagonist
Medium-dose ICS plus formoterol; if still not responding, high-dose ICS plus formoterol; then add ipratropium as the long-acting agent
questions.exp: Two 'Not responding' arrows take the protocol through 'medium-dose ICS + Formoterol' to 'High-dose ICS + Formoterol', and the next step is 'Add Tiotropium (LAMA: Long-acting muscarinic antagonist)'. Ipratropium is the SAMA of the ER chart on page 248. (Book p247)

questions.sec: Management: Inhaled Corticosteroids as Mainstay, the ICS–Formoterol Step Protocol with Biologics, and Investigations
questions.q: Match each biologic at the foot of the protocol with its printed target — 1) Omalizumab 2) Mepolizumab 3) Dupilumab, spelling as printed … A) Anti IL-4 receptor antagonist B) Anti-IgE C) Anti IL-5 receptor antagonist, description as printed
questions.exp: The biologics read 'Omalizumab (Anti-IgE)', 'mepolizumab (Anti IL-5 receptor antagonist)' and 'Dupilumab (Anti IL-4 receptor antagonist)', offered with a '+/−' after tiotropium. The IL-5-receptor description for mepolizumab and the 'Dupilumab' spelling are preserved as printed. (Book p247)

questions.sec: Management: Inhaled Corticosteroids as Mainstay, the ICS–Formoterol Step Protocol with Biologics, and Investigations
questions.q: Match each investigation on page 247 with its printed purpose and status — 1) Methacholine challenge test 2) Radioallergosorbent test, RAST 3) Fractional exhalation of NO … A) Measures IgE levels, braced as obsolete with its neighbour B) Assesses airway hyperresponsiveness, braced as obsolete with its neighbour C) Non-invasive test to measure airway inflammation
questions.exp: Methacholine challenge assesses airway hyperresponsiveness and RAST measures IgE levels, the two sharing the brace 'Obsolete', while fractional exhalation of NO stands below as the non-invasive test of airway inflammation. Methacholine also appeared as the challenge agent on page 191. (Book p247)

questions.sec: Management: Inhaled Corticosteroids as Mainstay, the ICS–Formoterol Step Protocol with Biologics, and Investigations
questions.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — three of these are printed ICS examples on page 247, one is a protocol partner drug instead:
opts: Formoterol
Fluticasone
Budesonide
Beclomethasone

units.title: General Features of Asthma, the Bronchodilator Reversibility Box, GINA Features and Respiratory Symptoms with Triggers
units.sec: General Features of Asthma, the Bronchodilator Reversibility Box, GINA Features and Respiratory Symptoms with Triggers
units.guide:
Asthma (p243) is a pure airway disease without parenchymal involvement — hence no hypercapnia, pulmonary HTN or cor-pulmonale — chronic, eosinophilic-inflammatory and reversibly bronchoconstricting.
Reversibility is tested with 4 puffs of SABA read at 30 minutes: an FEV1 rise of 12% plus 200 ml in absolute value is reversible (Asthma), its absence irreversible (COPD).
GINA features stack chronic airway inflammation with reversible bronchoconstriction, variable expiratory airflow obstruction and the symptoms shortness of breath, chronic cough, wheeze and chest tightness, which vary in time and intensity, worsen at night and with viral infections (RSV most common), and are triggered by exercise, laughter, allergens and cold air.

units.title: Etiopathogenesis: Triggers, Hygiene Hypothesis and TH2 Cytokines, Early versus Late Phases, and Eosinophil Mediators and Granules
units.sec: Etiopathogenesis: Triggers, Hygiene Hypothesis and TH2 Cytokines, Early versus Late Phases, and Eosinophil Mediators and Granules
units.guide:
Etiology is unknown (p244); triggers are URI, aspirin, beta blockers, sulfur dioxide, paint fumes, obesity, diet, 5q polymorphism and hyperventilation.
The hygiene hypothesis holds that increased childhood antigen exposure converts TH2 to TH1 cells for better immunity; TH2 products are IL-4 (raises IgE), IL-5 (recruits eosinophils via eotaxin) and IL-13, the early phase runs on histamine, tryptase and PGD2, and the late phase after 4–6 hours lists the basophil.
Eosinophils release newly synthesised membrane mediators (leukotriene B4, platelet activating factor, 15 HETE, prostaglandin E1/E2, thromboxane B2) and granule basic proteins MBP, ECP, EDN and EPO, with primary granules forming Charcot Leyden crystals and secondary granules holding MBP, ECP and EDN.

units.title: Histopathology of Asthma with Curschmann Spirals, the Extrinsic versus Intrinsic Table and Samter's Triad
units.sec: Histopathology of Asthma with Curschmann Spirals, the Extrinsic versus Intrinsic Table and Samter's Triad
units.guide:
Histopathology (p245) numbers chronic airway inflammation (eosinophils, mucus plugs, mast cells, Curschmann spirals — the captioned micrograph — and Charcot Leyden crystals), bronchial smooth muscle hypertrophy, submucosal glandular goblet-cell hyperplasia and patchy epithelial necrosis.
Extrinsic/atopic Asthma is allergy-associated with positive skin tests, raised IgE, family history, house dust mite (Dermatophagoids) etiology, childhood onset peaking at 3 years, equal sex ratio and a good prognosis as children grow out of it, against intrinsic Asthma with staphylococcal enterotoxins, adult onset, male predominance, severe persistent disease triggered by respiratory infections and a poor prognosis.
The closing Samters triad, as printed, triangles adult onset Asthma, aspirin sensitivity and nasal polyps.

units.title: Mild versus Moderate versus Severe Asthma Table and Acute Severe Exacerbation versus Impending Respiratory Failure
units.sec: Mild versus Moderate versus Severe Asthma Table and Acute Severe Exacerbation versus Impending Respiratory Failure
units.guide:
Intermittent Asthma stands apart while persistent Asthma grades mild, moderate and severe (p246): day symptoms 2–6 days/week → daily → continuous, nocturnal awakenings >2 monthly → >1/week → significantly reduced activity as printed, PEFR variability <30% → >30% → >30%, and FEV1 >80% → 60–80% → <60% predicted, under headers that carry over 'Extrinsic/atopic' and 'Intrinsic' from page 245.
An acute exacerbation speaks in words, is agitated and upright with ++ accessory use, loud wheeze, tachycardia, ++ pulsus paradoxus and PEFR 25–40 as printed, whereas impending respiratory failure is speechless, confused, unable to recline, with paradoxical breathing, silent chest, relative bradycardia, absent pulsus paradoxus and PEFR below 25.
Breathlessness at rest, tachypnoea, PaO2 below 60 mmHg (saturation below 90%) and PaCO2 below 40 mmHg are merged across both columns.

units.title: Management: Inhaled Corticosteroids as Mainstay, the ICS–Formoterol Step Protocol with Biologics, and Investigations
units.sec: Management: Inhaled Corticosteroids as Mainstay, the ICS–Formoterol Step Protocol with Biologics, and Investigations
units.guide:
ICS are the mainstay (p247), cutting hospitalisations, exacerbations and symptoms while improving lung function — early use improving future function — with beclomethasone, budesonide and fluticasone as examples, and SABA has no role in persistent Asthma.
The protocol steps from as-needed ICS–formoterol to daily low-dose ICS plus formoterol (preferred over ICS alone), then medium- and high-dose ICS plus formoterol for non-responders, then tiotropium (LAMA) with or without biologics omalizumab (anti-IgE), mepolizumab (printed anti-IL-5 receptor antagonist) and dupilumab (printed 'Dupilumab', anti-IL-4 receptor antagonist).
Methacholine challenge (airway hyperresponsiveness) and RAST (IgE levels) are braced obsolete, leaving fractional exhaled NO as the non-invasive measure of airway inflammation.

units.title: Management of Asthma Exacerbation in the ER and Brittle Asthma Types One and Two
units.sec: Management of Asthma Exacerbation in the ER and Brittle Asthma Types One and Two
units.guide:
The ER chart (p248) confirms the diagnosis and determines status: impending respiratory failure goes straight to intubation and ventilation, while acute severe Asthma receives nasal oxygen to SpO2 above 95%, albuterol 2.5–5 mg nebulised or 4–8 MDI puffs every 20 minutes, ipratropium 500 mg as printed and hydrocortisone 100 mg.
Reassessment at one hour by PEFR and oxygen saturation escalates the non-improver through IV MgSO4 2 g over 20 minutes and non-invasive ventilation to intubation.
Brittle Asthma is childhood Asthma: Type 1 shows wide peak-flow variation despite intense medication (multi-wave trace, oral corticosteroids) and Type 2 sudden severe exacerbations in otherwise well-controlled Asthma (single peak, subcutaneous adrenaline).
